title: Curated Misinformation: Liking Facebook Pages for Fake News Sites
screen_reason: Paired survey and Facebook digital-trace data from 806 US MTurk subjects (Dec 2016 - Jan 2017). Reports the share of subjects who liked at least one Facebook page for a fake-news website (18.36%), the share of liked pages that were fake-news pages (0.18% of 25,080 coded pages; per-subject means of 0.16% / 0.35%), the mean count of fake-news pages liked per subject, and a source-concentration figure (three lifestyle pages account for 23.9% of all fake-news page likes). All are quantitative shares with stated denominators from behavioural data.

estimates.date: Subjects completed the study between December 29, 2016 and January 2, 2017 (page likes are the cumulative set held at that date, covering the 2016 election cycle)
estimates.measure_type: % of subjects who liked at least one Facebook page for a fake news website
estimates.denominator: 806 American Facebook users recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk who completed the survey, installed the data-collection app and liked at least one content-coded page (828 completed, 22 dropped for having no codeable likes)
estimates.definition: Subject's set of liked Facebook pages contained at least one of the 46 pages matched to the Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news source list
estimates.misinfo_def: "Scholars generally agree that fake news is 'fabricated information that is patently false' (Molina et al., 2021) yet made to 'appear like real news' to readers (Tandoc et al., 2018). Fake news sources are classified at the level of the publisher"
estimates.source_quote: Among our 806 subjects, 18.36% (n = 148) liked at least one Facebook page for a fake news source, answering RQ1.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Liking Fake News Pages', p. 1297; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pages matched by name/URL (Python fuzzy match, >=65% character match reviewed manually) against the Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news source list, itself compiled from BuzzFeed, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, Snopes and academic lists (Allcott & Gentzkow 2017; Guess et al. 2019). Only pages liked by two or more respondents (25,080 of 141,693) were coded at all.
estimates.moderator_quote: This study relies on data from a convenience sample of MTurk participants who were willing to provide their Facebook data. This sample is non-representative of the American adult population (e.g., higher levels of education, which may result in a lower prevalence of fake news within the dataset). We do not suggest that results be used to extrapolate the overall rate of Facebook users who like fake news pages
estimates.notes: This is POTENTIAL exposure via feed curation, not observed exposure: the authors state 'because our data only track page likes and not the posts each page made or whether individual subjects saw those posts, we cannot know if subjects were actually exposed to fake news content'. reach_subtype = liking captures this. The authors explicitly warn against extrapolating the rate to the US population. The estimate is also a lower bound within its own frame: pages liked by only one respondent (116,613 of 141,693) were never coded.

estimates.measure_type: Mean % of a subject's total liked Facebook pages that were fake news pages
estimates.denominator: Each subject's total number of liked Facebook pages (mean 287.48 pages per subject, range 2-1,098), averaged across the 806 subjects
estimates.definition: Subject's count of liked fake-news pages divided by their total number of liked pages
estimates.misinfo_def: Pages for websites on the Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news publisher list
estimates.n: 806 persons (141,693 distinct pages liked in total)
estimates.source_quote: Fake news share of pages liked: Calculated by dividing subject's number of fake news pages liked by total number of pages liked. Calculated for all pages (M = 0.16%; SD = 0.79%; range = 0.00%-11.11%) and only coded pages (M = 0.35%; SD = 1.93%; range = 0.00%-33.33%).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news source list (BuzzFeed, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, Snopes and academic compilations)
estimates.moderator_quote: Facebook pages liked: M = 287.48; SD = 280.19; range = 2-1,098.
estimates.notes: Mean of a within-person share (not a pooled share). Denominator is ALL liked pages of any kind (brands, music, TV, etc.), so denom_scope = all_media rather than news_diet. Mechanically depressed because 116,613 uncoded singleton-liked pages sit in the denominator but could never enter the numerator.

estimates.measure_type: Mean % of a subject's content-CODED liked Facebook pages that were fake news pages
estimates.denominator: Each subject's liked pages that were among the 25,080 content-coded pages (those liked by two or more respondents), averaged across the 806 subjects
estimates.definition: Subject's count of liked fake-news pages divided by their number of liked pages that were content-coded
estimates.misinfo_def: Pages for websites on the Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news publisher list
estimates.source_quote: Calculated for all pages (M = 0.16%; SD = 0.79%; range = 0.00%-11.11%) and only coded pages (M = 0.35%; SD = 1.93%; range = 0.00%-33.33%).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news source list; denominator restricted to pages liked by two or more respondents, which were the only ones ever coded
estimates.moderator_quote: All pages liked by two or more respondents (n = 25,080) were coded for content type, partisan lean, and whether the page was a fake news source.
estimates.notes: Same measure as the 0.16% row with a narrower (curated) denominator, hence definition_variant = true. The 2.2x gap between 0.16% and 0.35% is purely a denominator artefact and is a clean illustration of how denominator choice moves a prevalence estimate.

estimates.measure_type: % of the content-coded Facebook pages liked by subjects that were pages for fake news websites
estimates.value_raw: 46, or 0.18% of pages analyzed (46 of 25,080 coded pages)
estimates.denominator: 25,080 distinct Facebook pages liked by two or more of the 806 subjects and coded for content type
estimates.definition: Page name/URL matched to an outlet on the Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news source list
estimates.misinfo_def: "Fake news sources are classified at the level of the publisher (Lazer et al., 2018); these outlets 'lack the news media's editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information'"
estimates.source_quote: This resulted in a total of 46 Facebook pages for fake news in the dataset, or 0.18% of all pages liked.
estimates.page_loc: Method, Fake News Page Coding, p. 1297; also p. 1291 ('46, or 0.18% of pages analyzed')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Python name-to-URL matching against the Grinberg et al. (2019) list with manual review of any >=65% character match; no reliability statistic given for the match review
estimates.moderator_quote: Respondents liked a total of 141,693 distinct Facebook pages. All pages liked by two or more respondents (n = 25,080) were coded for content type, partisan lean, and whether the page was a fake news source.
estimates.notes: borderline = true because the 'items' here are distinct pages deduplicated across users, so the figure is unweighted by how many people liked each page and is not the share of anyone's feed. Text says '0.18% of all pages liked' but 46/25,080 = 0.18%, i.e. the denominator is the 25,080 CODED pages, not the 141,693 pages actually liked (46/141,693 would be 0.03%). Authors note the count is a lower bound: pages that merely shared links to fake news sites were not counted, and Facebook had already removed some fake-news pages.

estimates.measure_type: Share of all fake-news page likes in the dataset accounted for by the three most popular fake-news pages (lifestyle sites)
estimates.value_raw: These three pages amount to 23.9% of fake news page likes in the dataset (The Mind Unleashed liked by 30 subjects, Collective Evolution by 20, David Wolfe by 15; 3 of the 46 fake news pages)
estimates.conc_group_label: The three most-liked fake news pages (3 of the 46 fake-news pages = 6.5% of fake-news sources): The Mind Unleashed, Collective Evolution, David Wolfe - all lifestyle sites that also published fake news
estimates.denominator: All fake-news page likes recorded in the dataset (likes by the 806 subjects on the 46 identified fake-news pages)
estimates.definition: Sum of subject-likes on the three named pages divided by the total number of fake-news page likes
estimates.misinfo_def: Pages for websites on the Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news publisher list
estimates.n: Fake-news page likes across 46 pages and 806 subjects (total count not stated)
estimates.source_quote: We consider three in particular: The Mind Unleashed, 9.2 million followers, liked by 30 subjects; Collective Evolution, 5.1 million followers, liked by 20 subjects; David Wolfe, 12.0 million followers, liked by 15 subjects. These three pages amount to 23.9% of fake news page likes in the dataset.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Liking Fake News Pages', pp. 1297-1298; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news source list
estimates.moderator_quote: A sizeable portion of page likes, 23.9%, came from three lifestyle sites that also published fake news articles during the 2016 cycle.
estimates.notes: Source-side concentration WITHIN fake news: the denominator is fake-news page likes only, in the same form as the Grinberg 1%-of-users/80%-of-exposure statistic the paper cites. conc_group_pct = 6.5 is 3/46 from two verbatim counts (three named pages; 'a total of 46 Facebook pages for fake news in the dataset'). If a coder prefers to express the group as a share of ALL 25,080 coded pages it would be 0.012% instead; the 3/46 framing is used because the activity denominator is fake-news likes.

estimates.measure_type: Mean number of fake-news Facebook pages liked per subject
estimates.denominator: 806 American Facebook users (MTurk convenience sample with app-collected page-like data)
estimates.definition: Count of pages on the Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news source list liked by each subject
estimates.misinfo_def: Pages for websites on the Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news publisher list
estimates.source_quote: On average, subjects liked fewer than one fake news pages (M = 0.37; median = 0); this echoes low levels of exposure in other studies
estimates.page_loc: Method, Dependent Variables, p. 1297; Discussion, p. 1302
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grinberg et al. (2019) fake-news source list
estimates.moderator_quote: Count of fake news pages: Number of fake news pages liked by each subject (median = 0; M = 0.37; SD = 1.15; range = 0-19).
estimates.notes: Per-capita intensity, not a share. Strong right skew (median 0, max 19); among the 148 subjects who liked any, the median was one page (82 liked one, 33 two, 17 three, 16 four or more). Note a small internal inconsistency: the Method reports range 0-19 while the Results section reports 'range = 0-18'.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Party-of-subject breakdowns of the headline rate (Independents 23.6%, Republicans 20.4%, Democrats 15.4%, other partisans 11.5%) are stated but are subgroup splits of the 18.36% figure rather than the paper's headline, so no rows were made; an adjudicator who reads the instruction's 'record subgroup rows only when they are the paper's headline, e.g. by party' more liberally could add four rows here. (2) '14.2% of subjects who liked any fake news' liked only the three lifestyle pages (21/148) is a composition statistic within the exposed subgroup, not a prevalence. (3) Footnote 7's '67.4% of Facebook pages for fake news sites were for right-leaning websites' and the ideology split of the 46 pages (17 right, 3 left, 14 other, 14 unavailable) describe ideology inside a misinformation-only set, not falsity, so R3 does not apply and no row was made. (4) Cluster-level shares in Table 2 (e.g. Cluster 2 holds 37.0% of fake news pages, Cluster 4 28.3%, Cluster 6 10.9%) are an audience-overlap partition of the 46 fake-news pages, not a prevalence or a top-group concentration of activity; not extracted. (5) All figures quoted from other studies in the literature review are excluded by R8: 71% who thought they saw made-up political news and 23% who thought they shared it (Barthel et al. 2016); '6% of total online news consumed' and '0.15% of Americans' average daily media consumption' (Allen et al. 2020); '44.3% of American adults are estimated to have visited a fake news site' (Guess et al. 2020); and, importantly for concentration, '1% of users accounted for 80% of exposure to fake news URLs' and '0.1% of users did 79.8% of the sharing' (Grinberg et al. 2019, quoted in text and footnote 2). (6) Regression coefficients in Table 1 are associations, not prevalences. (7) Judgement call for an adjudicator: sampling_frame was coded 'convenience' (the authors stress 'a convenience sample of MTurk participants' and warn against extrapolating), even though the misinformation measure itself comes from app-collected digital trace data, which would otherwise read as 'panel_trace'. If this codebook keys sampling_frame to the data modality rather than the recruitment, every row here should be re-coded panel_trace.

rob.design: Paired survey plus digital trace data. 828 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants completed a survey and consented to install an app that collected all Facebook pages they liked and their friend count, between 29 December 2016 and 2 January 2017; 22 were dropped for having no codeable page likes, leaving N = 806. Princeton University IRB approved. Self-described convenience sample, non-representative (more educated than the US adult population), with no response rate reported. Of the 141,693 distinct pages liked, only the 25,080 liked by two or more respondents were coded; topic coding was done by other MTurk workers, local/national and bias coding by student assistants and MTurk workers, and fake-news status by automated name-to-URL matching against the Grinberg et al. (2019) source list with manual review of near matches. No inter-coder reliability statistics are reported for any coding step. Regression via stepwise AIC selection (logistic, Poisson with robust SEs, OLS). Key measurement limitation acknowledged by the authors: page likes are potential, not observed, exposure - they do not observe the pages' posts or whether subjects saw them.
rob.item6_quote: The 25,080 topic-coded Facebook pages were coded as a fake news source if they matched a URL in the Grinberg et al. (2019) source list, which itself is a compilation of fake news sources identified by Buzzfeed, Politifact, FactCheck.org, and Snopes.com as well as academics (Allcott & Gentzkow, 2017; A. Guess et al., 2019).
rob.item10_quote: Among our 806 subjects, 18.36% (n = 148) liked at least one Facebook page for a fake news source, answering RQ1.
